summary: Specifies an initial set of identifiers for the MPLS Transport Profile. MPLS-TP must be configurable and manageable without a control plane, so it needs consistent naming conventions for nodes, links, and paths used in management and operations.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC works out how to name everything in an MPLS Transport Profile network: the routers, their ports, the tunnels between them, the paths inside those tunnels, and the points used for maintenance checks. The names are built from a few simple pieces so that two providers can use the same numbers without colliding.

subtitle: Naming conventions for the nodes, interfaces, tunnels, paths and maintenance points of an MPLS Transport Profile network.

tldr.problem: MPLS-TP must be configurable and manageable without a control plane, so operators and tools need a consistent way to name the elements and objects in the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC builds identifiers from a few pieces: a Global_ID taken from the operator's AS number, a 32-bit Node_ID, an interface number, tunnel and LSP numbers, and pseudowire attachment identifiers. These are combined with the :: notation and are compatible with IP, MPLS, GMPLS and pseudowire conventions.
tldr.outcome: Management and OAM functions get one shared naming scheme, including identifiers for maintenance entity groups and their end and intermediate points. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Global_ID
facts.value: Unsigned 32-bit, derived from a 4-octet AS number

today: RFC 6370 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2011. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. The document describes an information model, and says that the protocol specifications that use it must describe their own security and authentication concerns.

sections.title: Why MPLS-TP Needs Names
sections.content:
The document specifies an initial set of identifiers to be used in the Transport Profile of Multiprotocol Label Switching. The MPLS-TP requirements in RFC 5654 require that the elements and objects in an MPLS-TP environment can be configured and managed without a control plane, and in such an environment many conventions for defining identifiers are possible. This document defines identifiers for MPLS-TP management and operations, administration and maintenance functions, compatible with IP and MPLS conventions: the identifiers have been chosen to be compatible with existing IP, MPLS, GMPLS and pseudowire definitions.

The document is a product of a joint IETF and ITU-T effort to include an MPLS Transport Profile within the IETF MPLS and PWE3 architectures, to support the capabilities of a packet transport network as defined by the ITU-T.

To configure, operate and manage such a network, a number of entities require identification, and this document defines identifiers for the Global_ID, the Node, the Interface, the Tunnel, the LSP, the PW, the MEG, the MEP and the MIP. The term tunnel is borrowed from RSVP-TE, where it describes an entity that provides a logical association between a source and destination LSR. The tunnel is instantiated by one or more LSPs, where the additional LSPs are used for protection or re-grooming of the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: An MPLS Transport Profile network is meant to be run like a traditional transport network: configured and maintained by hand and by management tools, without a routing protocol doing the work. For that, every box and every path needs a name that means the same thing to every tool.

sections.title: How the Names Are Written
sections.content:
All multiple-word atomic identifiers use underscores to join the words. Many identifiers are composed of a set of other identifiers, expressed by listing them joined with double-colon notation. Where the same identifier type is used more than once in a concatenation, it is qualified by a prefix joined to the identifier by a dash, so that A1-Node_ID is the Node_ID of a node referred to as A1.

The notation also defines a preferred ordering of the fields. The designation A1 indicates the lower sort order of a field or set of fields, and Z9 indicates the higher sort order of the same, with the sort being alphanumeric or numeric depending on the field's definition. Where the sort applies to a group of fields, those fields are grouped with braces.

The uniqueness of an identifier does not depend on the ordering, but on the uniqueness and scoping of the fields that compose it. The preferred ordering is not intended to constrain protocol designs by dictating a particular field sequence or even what fields appear in which objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Two conventions run through all the names. Underscores join the words of one name, and double colons join separate names. The A1 and Z9 markers say which end of a link comes first, so that both ends of a connection write the same name.

sections.title: The Global_ID
sections.content:
The Global_ID uniquely identifies an operator. RFC 5003 defines a globally unique Attachment Interface Identifier, composed of three parts: a Global_ID that uniquely identifies an operator, a prefix, and finally an attachment circuit identifier, and that Global ID is used here for MPLS-TP. Quoting from RFC 5003, the global ID can contain the 2-octet or 4-octet value of the provider's Autonomous System Number, and it is expected that the global ID will be derived from the globally unique ASN of the autonomous system hosting the PEs that contain the actual AIIs. The presence of a global ID based on the operator's ASN ensures that the AII is globally unique.

A Global_ID is an unsigned 32-bit value and MUST be derived from a 4-octet AS number assigned to the operator. 2-octet AS numbers have been incorporated in the 4-octet form by placing the 2-octet AS number in the low-order octets and setting the two high-order octets to zero. ASN 0 is reserved and cannot be assigned to an operator, and an identifier containing a Global_ID of zero means that no Global_ID is specified. A Global_ID of zero is limited to entities contained within a single operator and MUST NOT be used across a network-to-network interface.

The Global_ID is used solely to provide a globally unique context for other MPLS-TP identifiers. While the AS number used in the Global_ID MUST be one that the operator is entitled to use, the use of the Global_ID is not related to the use of the ASN in protocols such as BGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Every name can be prefixed with the provider's own autonomous system number. That number is unique across the Internet, so prefixing with it makes the name unique everywhere, not just inside one operator's network.

sections.title: Nodes and Interfaces
sections.content:
An LSR requires identification of the node itself and of its interfaces. An interface is the attachment point to a server sub-layer, for example an MPLS-TP section or an MPLS-TP tunnel. The identifier associated with a node is the Node Identifier, a unique 32-bit value assigned by the operator within the scope of a Global_ID. The structure of the Node_ID is operator-specific and outside the scope of this document, but the value zero is reserved and MUST NOT be used. Where IPv4 addresses are used it may be convenient to use the node's IPv4 loopback address as the Node_ID, though the Node_ID does not need to have any association with the IPv4 address space used in the operator's IGP or EGP. Where IPv6 addresses are used exclusively, a 32-bit value unique within the scope of a Global_ID is assigned.

An LSR can support multiple layers, for example hierarchical LSPs, and the Node_ID belongs to the multiple-layer context: it applies to all LSPs or PWs that originate on, have an intermediate point on, or terminate on the node. Where a Node_ID needs to be globally unique, this is accomplished by prefixing it with the operator's Global_ID.

The term interface is used for the attachment point to an MPLS-TP section. Within the context of a particular node, the identifier associated with an interface is an Interface Number, a 32-bit unsigned integer assigned by the operator that MUST be unique within the scope of a Node_ID. The value 0 has special meaning for MIP identifiers and MUST NOT be used to identify an MPLS-TP interface. The IF_Num has no relation with the ifNum object defined in RFC 2863, and no mapping is mandated between IF_Num and ifIndex.

An Interface Identifier identifies an interface uniquely within the context of a Global_ID. It is formed by concatenating the Node_ID with the IF_Num, so an IF_ID is a 64-bit identifier written as Node_ID::IF_Num. This convention was chosen to allow compatibility with GMPLS, whose signaling functional description requires interface identification and allows three formats for the Interface_ID, the third being an IPv4 address plus a 32-bit unsigned integer for the specific interface. The format defined for MPLS-TP is consistent with that format but uses the Node_ID instead of an IPv4 address.
sections.plainLanguage: A router gets a 32-bit number from its operator, and each of its ports gets a number of its own. Together they name a port uniquely, in the same way that a street number names a door on a street.

sections.title: Tunnels, Paths and the RSVP Mapping
sections.content:
In MPLS the actual transport of packets is provided by LSPs, and a transport service may be composed of several LSPs, with the LSPs providing the service changing over time because of protection and restoration events. To identify the service clearly, the term MPLS-TP Tunnel is used for a service provided by, for example, a working LSP protected by a protection LSP. The Tunnel Identifier identifies the transport service and provides a stable binding to the client in the face of changes in the data-plane LSPs used to provide the service.

At each end point a tunnel is uniquely identified by the end point's Node_ID and a locally assigned tunnel number. A Tunnel Number is a 16-bit unsigned integer unique within the context of the Node_ID. Each end point having its own tunnel number allows a compact form for the MEP_ID and simplifies other signaling, such as the setup of associated bidirectional tunnels. The concatenation of the two end point identifiers serves as the full identifier, and the format of a Tunnel_ID is A1-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}::Z9-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}. Where it needs to be globally unique, globally unique Node_IDs are used, giving A1-{Global_ID::Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}::Z9-{Global_ID::Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}. When an MPLS-TP Tunnel is configured it MUST be assigned a unique IF_ID at each end point.

An LSP Number is a 16-bit unsigned integer. For a co-routed bidirectional LSP, which is composed of two unidirectional LSPs traversing the same links in opposite directions and provisioned or signaled as a single entity, a single LSP number is used within the scope of the MPLS-TP Tunnel_ID, and the format of the LSP_ID is A1-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}::Z9-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num}::LSP_Num. The ordering does not matter for uniqueness, so the reversed form is synonymous. For an associated bidirectional LSP, where the two unidirectional LSPs are separate, each direction requires its own LSP_Num, and the format is A1-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num::LSP_Num}::Z9-{Node_ID::Tunnel_Num::LSP_Num}. Sub-Path Maintenance Entities, as defined in RFC 5921, are also LSPs and use these same forms of identifiers.

Section 5.3 maps an MPLS-TP LSP_ID to RSVP-TE, and is informative. GMPLS and RSVP-TE signaling use a 5-tuple to identify an LSP within an operator's network, composed of the Tunnel End-point Address, the Tunnel_ID, the Extended Tunnel ID, the Tunnel Sender Address and the RSVP LSP_ID. For a co-routed bidirectional LSP signaled from A1 to Z9, the mapping is that the Tunnel End-point Address is Z9-Node_ID, the Tunnel_ID is A1-Tunnel_Num, the Extended Tunnel_ID is A1-Node_ID, the Tunnel Sender Address is A1-Node_ID and the RSVP LSP_ID is LSP_Num. RSVP-TE has yet to be extended to accommodate Global_IDs, so the mapping is made only for the network-unique form of the LSP_ID and assumes the operator has derived its Node_IDs from valid IPv4 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel names the service the customer sees, and it keeps that name even when the path inside it is rerouted. Under the tunnel sits the path itself, identified by a number, and for a path that runs both ways there are two ways to write the name depending on whether the two directions share a route.

sections.title: Pseudowire Path Identifiers
sections.content:
Pseudowire signaling defines two FECs used to signal pseudowires, and of these the Generalized PWid FEC, type 129, along with AII Type 2 as defined in RFC 5003, fits the identification requirements of MPLS-TP. In an MPLS-TP environment a PW is identified by a set of identifiers that can be mapped directly to those elements, and to distinguish it from other pseudowire identifiers this is called a Pseudowire Path Identifier.

The AII Type 2 is composed of three fields: the Global_ID, the Prefix and the AC_ID. The Global_ID used here is identical to the one defined in RFC 5003, the Node_ID is used as the Prefix, and the AC_ID is as defined in RFC 5003. To complete the Generalized PWid FEC all that is required is an Attachment Group Identifier, exactly as specified in RFC 4447.

A bidirectional pseudowire consists of a pair of unidirectional LSPs, one in each direction, so the Generalized PWid FEC has a notion of Source AII and Target AII. These terms are used relative to the direction of the LSP: the SAII is assigned to the end that allocates the PW label for a given direction, and the TAII to the other end. In a purely configured environment, when referring to the entire PW, that distinction is not critical, and a Generalized PWid FEC of AGIa::AIIb::AIIc is equivalent to AGIa::AIIc::AIIb. In a signaled environment the convention in RFC 4447 is that at a particular end point the AII associated with that end point comes first. The complete PW_Path_ID is AGI::A1-{Global_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID}::Z9-{Global_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID}.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire, which is a service carried across a network as if the two ends were directly connected, gets a name built from the same pieces: the operator's number, the router at each end, and the circuit number at each end.

sections.title: Maintenance Identifiers
sections.content:
In MPLS-TP a Maintenance Entity Group represents an entity that requires management and defines a relationship between a set of maintenance points. A maintenance point is either a Maintenance Entity Group End Point, a Maintenance Entity Group Intermediate Point, or a Pseudowire Segment End Point. Within the context of a MEG, MEPs and MIPs must be uniquely identified.

MEG identifiers are required for MPLS-TP sections, LSPs and pseudowires, and the formats follow the IP-compatible identifiers defined earlier. For MPLS-TP sections at layer 0, the MEG_ID is formed by concatenating the two IF_IDs of the section using the A1/Z9 ordering, A1-IF_ID::Z9-IF_ID, and the globally unique form is A1-{Global_ID::IF_ID}::Z9-{Global_ID::IF_ID}. Sections above layer 0 are LSPs and use their LSP MEG IDs. For LSPs, the MEG_ID is simply the corresponding LSP_ID with the A1/Z9 ordering, and for pseudowires the MEG_ID is the corresponding PW_Path_ID. The RFC notes that while these identifiers are syntactically identical to the LSP_ID and PW_Path_ID, they have different semantics, so different types need to be assigned if both are encoded in TLVs.

For MEP identifiers, the MEP_IDs of MPLS-TP sections at layer 0 are the IF_IDs of each end of the section, and the globally unique form is Global_ID::IF_ID. The LSP_MEP_ID is Node_ID::Tunnel_Num::LSP_Num, where the Node_ID is the node in which the MEP is located and the Tunnel_Num is the tunnel number unique to that node, with a single LSP_Num used at both ends of a co-routed bidirectional LSP and the direction-specific LSP_Num used for an associated one. The globally unique form is Global_ID::Node_ID::Tunnel_Num::LSP_Num. For pseudowires, a MEP_ID takes the form AGI::Global_ID::Node_ID::AC_ID.

For a MIP associated with a particular interface, the IF_ID of the cross-connected interfaces is used, which allows MIPs to be independently identified in one node where a per-interface MIP model is used. If only a per-node MIP model is used, one MIP is configured, and the MIP_ID is formed from the Node_ID and an IF_Num of 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Maintenance checks, such as testing that a path still carries traffic, need to name the ends of the path and the middle. The RFC gives each of those a name derived from the identifiers already defined.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes an information model and, as such, does not introduce security concerns. Protocol specifications that describe use of this information model may introduce security risks and concerns about authentication of participants, so the writers of protocol specifications for the purpose of describing implementation of this information model need to describe the security and authentication concerns that may be raised by the particular mechanisms defined and how those concerns may be addressed.

Uniqueness of the identifiers is guaranteed by the assigner: a Global_ID is unique based on the assignment of ASNs from IANA, and both a Node_ID and an IF_Num are unique based on assignment by an operator. Failure by an assigner to use unique values within the specified scoping could result in operational problems, for example a non-unique MEP value could result in failure to detect a mis-merged LSP.

Protocol specifications that use the identifiers defined here need to consider the implications of guessable identifiers and, where there is a security implication, SHOULD give advice on how to make identifiers less guessable.
sections.plainLanguage: Naming things does not by itself create a security risk, but the protocols built on these names have to authenticate each other and should avoid names an attacker could guess.
